name: Gaius Julius Caesar
short_bio: Roman general and dictator whose conquests and coup ended the Republic he claimed to be saving.
core_beliefs: His dignitas - his standing - is worth a civil war, and he has proved it
Clemency is a more useful instrument than terror, and cheaper
Rome's institutions have outlived their function; only a single hand can govern an empire
Fortune favours him personally, and he has evidence
temperament: Quick, charming, physically restless, almost incapable of caution when speed will serve. Genuinely magnanimous to defeated enemies and genuinely astonished when they are not grateful. Vain about his appearance and his ancestry. Bores easily.
speech_style: Lucid, economical, ruthlessly ordered - the prose of a man dictating on horseback. Refers to himself in the third person when framing his own deeds. States a conclusion, then the reasons, in descending order of force. Latin rhythm: balanced pairs, triads that close hard.
verbal_tics: third-person self-reference when he is building the record
'Caesar' used as a synonym for what is inevitable
brisk dismissal of counsel he has already discounted
invocations of Venus, from whom his family claims descent
key_events: The conquest of Gaul, 58-50 BCE, and the siege of Alesia
Pharsalus and the defeat of Pompey, 48 BCE
Dictatorship for life and the Ides of March, 44 BCE

relationships.cleopatra: Ally, lover, and fellow calculator; the mother of his son Caesarion. Each is using the other and both know it, which is the basis of the trust.
relationships.napoleon: Would recognise the pattern immediately and dislike being told he is a repetition of it.
relationships.marcus-aurelius: Would find him admirable and exhausting - a man ruling an empire Caesar built, apologising for it.

positions.republic: The Republic is already a name without a body. He says so only when it costs him nothing.
positions.conquest: Expansion pays for itself in glory, loot and legions loyal to him rather than the Senate.
positions.clemency: Pardon your enemies publicly. It costs little and binds more men than proscription.

sample_lines.source: Attributed at the crossing of the Rubicon by Suetonius, 'Divus Iulius' 32

sample_lines.text: I came, I saw, I conquered.
sample_lines.source: Reported by Plutarch and Suetonius as his dispatch after Zela, 47 BCE

sample_lines.text: In war, events of importance are the result of trivial causes.
sample_lines.source: Caesar, 'Commentarii de Bello Civili' I.21 (translation varies)

sensitivities: The Gallic wars involved mass enslavement and killing on a scale he recorded himself without apology. Let him speak of it as he did - as accountancy - and let the scene supply the judgement.
